screens.title: Bluetooth and Wi‑Fi Modules
screens.narratorSegment: Wireless communication is the step that turns an Arduino project into an Internet of Things device. In this chapter you'll learn how simple serial Bluetooth modules like the HC-05 and HC-06 behave like ordinary serial ports, how to wire and talk to them safely, and how to use an ESP8266 or ESP32 board when you need built‑in Wi‑Fi. We'll walk through the hands‑on flow: wiring a Bluetooth module, pairing it with a phone, sending on/off commands, and then contrast that with running a tiny web server on an ESP board to control an LED from a browser. You'll also learn the security basics you must consider before exposing controls over the air, including why hard‑coding passwords is fine for experiments but risky for real devices. To ground learning, there are concrete examples: a Bluetooth controlled LED using simple serial commands, and the minimal ESP8266 web server sketch that serves a control page. As you go through each lesson, notice a common tradeoff: Bluetooth modules are simple and low cost; ESP boards offer more memory and network features. Think about which option matches your project goals and what security steps you would add before deploying.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you will be able to add simple wireless control to a microcontroller project, and you will know when to choose Bluetooth or a Wi‑Fi board. First, you will connect an HC‑05 or HC‑06 to an Arduino and treat it as a serial device, using the same send and receive functions you already know. That skill matters because it lets you control pins and devices from a phone without changing how your sketch parses input. Second, you will set up SoftwareSerial when the hardware serial pins are reserved for USB programming, a practical workaround that prevents conflicts during development. Third, you will identify when an ESP8266 or ESP32 board is the better platform — these boards have built‑in Wi‑Fi and more memory, so they run web servers and handle networked logic more easily. Finally, you will apply basic IoT security checks: avoid exposing unauthenticated controls, avoid publishing hard‑coded credentials in production, and plan for firmware updates. Each objective includes a short hands‑on checkpoint so you can confirm competency as you build.

screens.title: Objective Deep Dive
screens.narratorSegment: Let's map the objectives to real project actions so you understand why each skill matters. When you link an HC‑05 to an Arduino, you are exposing the same serial input path used by the USB monitor, but now the input can come from a phone. That means your parsing code stays the same and your UI options expand to mobile apps and inexpensive Bluetooth terminals. SoftwareSerial matters because pins zero and one are commonly used for USB programming; if you accidentally wire a Bluetooth TX to the hardware RX while uploading sketches you may block uploads or get confusing serial data. Choosing an ESP8266 or ESP32 replaces the Uno plus wireless add‑on pattern with a single board that has built‑in Wi‑Fi and more memory. That simplifies web server projects and frees you from bridging serial links. Finally, the security objective ties everything together: whether you control an LED over Bluetooth or a web page, exposing unauthenticated control to the public internet is risky. Practically, we will test each objective with a hands‑on exercise and a small verification step so you can confirm competency.

screens.title: Bluetooth modules behave like serial ports
screens.narratorSegment: A Bluetooth module such as the HC‑05 or HC‑06 acts like a wireless serial cable. In practice this means you can use the same send and receive routines you already use with USB: the print function to send text and the read functions to receive it. Concretely, if your sketch looks for the string on to switch an LED on, you can keep that logic unchanged and have a phone send the string instead of the Serial Monitor. This is powerful because it separates the transport from your application logic. A common misconception is that Bluetooth modules require special wireless APIs; they do not — they simply forward bytes over a radio link. One caution: the HC‑05 has pins labeled VCC, GND, TXD, RXD, EN, and STATE, and TX/RX lines operate at microcontroller logic levels. If you wire TXD directly into a 5V Arduino RX without a level check you may risk damage; use a simple voltage divider when required. Example: sending the characters "on" from a phone terminal app can trigger the same conditional code you use for a typed command. Takeaway: treat Bluetooth modules as serial wires that happen to be wireless, and mind pin voltages and hardware serial conflicts as you wire and program.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.3 › Bluetooth modules behave like serial ports
Core Concept
HC‑05 / HC‑06 as serial devices
They send and receive bytes exactly like a wired serial connection. Your sketch parses the same data patterns.
Key points
  • Use Serial.print and Serial.read semantics through the module.
  • TXD/RXD map to Arduino RX/TX; watch for voltage level compatibility.
  • EN and STATE pins offer enable and status indicators but are optional for basic use.
Example
A phone terminal sends the characters "on" to the module. Your parsed conditional turns on an LED the same way it would when typing into the Serial Monitor.
Common mistake
Wiring TX and RX to hardware serial pins while uploading sketches can block the USB serial connection and cause confusing upload failures.
Wiring snapshot
Pin mapping
VCC → 5V, GND → GND, TXD → Arduino RX (use divider if needed), RXD → Arduino TX. EN and STATE optional for advanced use.
Practical tip
When pins zero and one are used for USB programming, prefer SoftwareSerial on other pins to avoid conflicts.
Analogy
Think of the module as a wireless serial cable: the bytes don't care how they're transported, only what they contain.
Key Takeaway

Use existing serial parsing logic with Bluetooth, but always check pin levels and avoid serial conflicts during uploads.

screens.title: HC‑05 / HC‑06 pin roles and safe wiring
screens.narratorSegment: Wiring a Bluetooth module correctly keeps your hardware safe and your project reliable. The HC‑05 typically exposes six pins: VCC, GND, TXD, RXD, EN, and STATE. VCC powers the module; GND is the common reference. TXD transmits bytes from the module and connects to the Arduino receive pin; RXD receives bytes from the Arduino and connects to the Arduino transmit pin. A practical safety step is checking voltage levels: many Arduino boards use five volt logic while some Bluetooth modules expect three point three volts. That means you should use a simple voltage divider on the Arduino TX line going to RXD when required, or ensure the module tolerates five volts. The EN pin can be used to enable or disable the module, useful in power management, and STATE provides a status output that some projects use to detect pairing. A common wiring mistake is swapping TX and RX incorrectly or powering the module with the wrong voltage. Example wiring: VCC to 5V, GND to ground, TXD to Arduino RX via direct or divider as required, RXD to Arduino TX — but if you plan to upload sketches, avoid pins zero and one and use SoftwareSerial on other digital pins. Takeaway: double‑check pin labels, voltage, and choose SoftwareSerial when USB programming must remain available.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.3 › HC‑05 / HC‑06 pin roles and safe wiring
Definition
Pin roles and wiring checklist
A concise wiring checklist and protection tips to avoid common hardware mistakes.
VCC & GND
Power the module with the correct voltage. Many setups use 5V supply but check datasheet if unsure.
TXD / RXD
TXD goes to Arduino RX; RXD goes to Arduino TX. Use a level shifter or voltage divider if the logic levels differ.
EN
Optional enable pin to turn the module on or off in power sensitive projects.
STATE
Status output that can tell you if the module is paired or connected.
Pro tip
If you plan to upload sketches frequently, wire TX/RX to SoftwareSerial pins so hardware serial remains free for the bootloader and USB programming.
Wiring Example
A common safe wiring pattern and a quick checklist to run before power up.
Checklist
  • Confirm module VCC rating before applying power.
  • Place a voltage divider on Arduino TX if module is 3.3V only.
  • Swap TX/RX for correct direction of data flow.
  • Test pairing with a phone app before wiring outputs.
Analogy
Think of TX as someone talking and RX as someone listening; flipping them stops the conversation.
Key Takeaway

Correct pin mapping and level protection prevent damage and make development smoother.

screens.title: SoftwareSerial and avoiding USB conflicts
screens.narratorSegment: Hardware serial pins on many Arduino models are shared with the USB interface, so a popular pattern is to use SoftwareSerial or similar libraries to move Bluetooth communication to other digital pins. The core idea is simple: create a secondary serial object attached to two free digital pins, and read and write to it just like the hardware serial. This lets the USB port remain free for programming and for the Serial Monitor so you can debug while the Bluetooth module runs in parallel. A common mistake is assuming SoftwareSerial works at very high baud rates; performance can degrade, so test your chosen baud and reduce it if you see dropped characters. Example process: choose two free pins, initialize SoftwareSerial at the module's baud rate, swap TX/RX as needed, then implement the same parsing logic you use for Serial. Why it matters: using SoftwareSerial prevents upload conflicts and keeps your development loop fast. Misconception check: SoftwareSerial is not faster or more reliable than hardware serial; it's a practical workaround for development convenience. Takeaway: use SoftwareSerial for development when hardware serial is busy, and verify stability at your chosen baud rate before finalizing wiring.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.3 › SoftwareSerial and avoiding USB conflicts
Process Flow
Set up SoftwareSerial
Stepwise checklist to move Bluetooth off the hardware RX/TX pins and preserve USB programming.
  1. Pick two free digital pins for RX and TX and wire them to the module.
  2. Include the SoftwareSerial library and create an instance at the module baud rate.
  3. Use the SoftwareSerial instance to read and write bytes; keep hardware Serial for debugging and uploads.
  4. Test communication and reduce baud if characters are lost.
Common mistake
Expecting SoftwareSerial to match hardware serial performance at high baud rates; measure and adjust.
Concrete Example
Create a SoftwareSerial on pins 10 and 11, initialize it at the same baud as the Bluetooth module, and forward parsing logic from the hardware Serial to the SoftwareSerial instance. Confirm you can upload sketches while the module is connected.
Why this matters
It prevents accidental blocking of the bootloader and keeps the USB Serial Monitor available for troubleshooting while your Bluetooth link remains active.
Key Takeaway

Use SoftwareSerial to avoid serial conflicts, and test baud reliability before committing to wiring.

screens.title: Pairing and command flow from a smartphone
screens.narratorSegment: Pairing an HC‑05 or HC‑06 with a smartphone creates a virtual serial link that your phone can send strings over. The typical flow is: power the module, make it discoverable or enter pairing mode, pair from the phone using a Bluetooth terminal app, then open a terminal to send commands. In many learning projects you will send short commands like "on" and "off" or single characters like "1" and "0" to represent states. Your sketch looks for those exact strings and sets digital outputs accordingly. A practical example: if you send the character "1" the sketch sets an LED pin HIGH; if you send "0" the sketch sets it LOW. A common misconception is that pairing alone secures control; it does not prevent someone already paired from sending dangerous commands. For this reason, keep critical controls on authenticated channels or limit pairing range when possible. When testing, start with simple commands, confirm the LED or relay responds, and then expand to richer command parsing only after you validate reliability. Takeaway: pairing creates convenience but not full security — start simple, then plan safeguards.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.3 › Pairing and command flow from a smartphone
Process Flow
Pair → Open Terminal → Send Commands
Simple controlled sequence for turning an LED on and off from a smartphone terminal app.
Step 1
Power and make module discoverable, then pair from the phone using the default PIN if required.
Step 2
Open a Bluetooth terminal app and connect to the module's virtual serial port.
Step 3
Send "1" to set LED high and "0" to set it low. Confirm action is immediate and reliable.
Concrete example
Send the character 1 from the phone. Your parsing code treats that character as a command to set the LED pin HIGH and returns an acknowledgment if your sketch sends one.
Security note
Paired devices can send commands freely. For sensitive controls, plan authentication or limit access by keeping devices in private environments.
Key Takeaway

Pairing is convenient for control but does not replace secure authentication; start with short commands and verify behavior.

screens.title: Uno plus ESP8266 vs ESP8266/ESP32 boards
screens.narratorSegment: The Arduino Uno itself lacks built‑in Wi‑Fi. You have two common paths to add network capability: connect an ESP8266 module to an Uno, or use an ESP8266‑based board such as NodeMCU or a Wemos D1 Mini, or choose an ESP32 board. The key tradeoffs are convenience, resources, and complexity. An Uno with an ESP8266 add‑on keeps your familiar Uno environment but adds wiring, serial bridging, and potential baud or pin conflicts. By contrast, using a NodeMCU or ESP32 replaces the Uno with a single board that already has Wi‑Fi, more memory, and higher speed. That makes serving web pages and handling network logic simpler and more robust. A common misconception is that the Uno plus module and the NodeMCU are identical experiences; they are not — the latter simplifies networking and avoids bridging problems. Example: an ESP board can run the same Arduino language sketches and libraries while offering a built‑in network stack to host a web server. Practical guidance: prefer ESP boards for web server projects and when you need memory and speed; use an Uno plus ESP module if you have peripherals tied to the Uno and need minimal wireless features. Takeaway: choose the architecture that matches your resource, wiring, and deployment needs.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.3 › Uno plus ESP8266 vs ESP8266/ESP32 boards
Comparison
Uno + ESP8266 vs ESP Boards
Side‑by‑side tradeoffs to guide board selection.
Uno + ESP8266
Keeps existing Uno peripherals, but requires serial bridging, extra wiring, and can complicate uploads and debugging.
NodeMCU / Wemos / ESP32
Single board with built‑in Wi‑Fi, more memory, higher speed, and native networking APIs — ideal for web server projects.
Concrete example
The same sketch structure and Arduino APIs can be used on an ESP board, but you remove the serial bridge and use the built‑in Wi‑Fi stack to serve pages.
Misconception check
Do not assume an Uno plus module will behave exactly like an ESP board; resources and networking are different.
Key Takeaway

For web servers and heavier network logic, prefer an ESP board. For small wireless add‑ons that reuse an Uno, an ESP8266 module can work but adds wiring complexity.

screens.title: Minimal ESP8266 web server example
screens.narratorSegment: A simple and instructive Wi‑Fi project is running a minimal web server on an ESP8266 to control an LED. The provided sketch shows the essential steps: include the Wi‑Fi and server libraries, provide network credentials, wait for a connection, register a handler for the root path, and start the server loop. The sketch sets the LED pin as output, connects to the network using the provided network name and password, waits until the board reports it is connected, and then registers a handler function for the root URL that sends a web page with on/off controls. content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.3 › Minimal ESP8266 web server example
Code Walkthrough
ESP8266 web server skeleton
Key areas: libraries, credentials, connection loop, handler registration, server loop.
#include <ESP8266WiFi.h>
#include <WiFiClient.h>
#include <ESP8266WebServer.h>

const char* ssid = "YourNetwork";
const char* password = "YourPassword";
ESP8266WebServer server(80);

void setup() {
  pinMode(LED_BUILTIN, OUTPUT);
  WiFi.begin(ssid, password);
  while (WiFi.status() != WL_CONNECTED) {
    delay(500);
  }
  server.on("/", handleRoot);
  server.begin();
}

void loop() {
  server.handleClient();
}
Practical note
This sketch demonstrates the bare essentials. Expand the root handler to include on/off controls that write to the LED pin when links or buttons are clicked.
Concrete scenario
After connecting to Wi‑Fi, browse to the board's IP and click an on/off link that your handler maps to digital writes for the LED.
Security reminder
Hard‑coded credentials are fine for experiments; avoid publishing such sketches for deployed devices and consider authentication if opening endpoints.
Key Takeaway

The ESP8266 can host a simple web server with a few library calls, making browser‑based control straightforward for prototyping.

screens.title: Programming ESP boards with the Arduino IDE
screens.narratorSegment: ESP8266 and ESP32 boards are programmable with the Arduino IDE using the same language and many of the same libraries. That means you can transfer your existing Arduino knowledge directly to an ESP board while gaining access to networking functions and more memory. Programming flow remains familiar: select the board in the IDE, include the required Wi‑Fi libraries, and upload. A practical implication is that learning how to write handlers, parse requests, and toggle pins transfers smoothly. One common issue learners face is board selection and drivers; ensure you choose the correct target board in the IDE and confirm the USB driver is present. Another misconception is that libraries behave identically across AVR‑based Arduinos and ESP architectures; some timing and hardware‑specific libraries may differ, so test peripheral code. Example: the minimal web server sketch uses the ESP8266WiFi and ESP8266WebServer libraries that are specific to that platform. Takeaway: you get the convenience of the Arduino programming model with added networking APIs, but always validate library compatibility when moving sketches between boards. screens.title: IoT security basics for wireless projects
screens.narratorSegment: Security should be part of your design thinking when you move from bench prototypes to deployed devices. Hard‑coding Wi‑Fi passwords directly in sketches is common and convenient for learning, but it creates a risk if the sketch is shared or the device is connected to a larger network. The basic safeguards to consider are: prefer encrypted endpoints when possible, protect control interfaces with authentication so only trusted clients can issue commands, and keep firmware regularly updated to patch vulnerabilities. A frequent misconception is that small devices are too trivial to be targeted; in practice any exposed interface can be abused if left unauthenticated. Example actions: do not expose unauthenticated control pages to the public internet; if you must remote access a device, use authentication or place the device behind a protected network. For Bluetooth, remember pairing is not the same as authentication against an application server — paired devices can still send commands. Takeaway: for prototypes, hard‑coding is fine for learning. screens.title: Build a Bluetooth‑controlled LED
screens.narratorSegment: This hands‑on exercise walks you through a compact project: a Bluetooth‑controlled LED. The goal is to pair an HC‑06 with your phone and send 1 to turn the LED on and 0 to turn it off. Start by wiring power and ground, and connect TXD and RXD to the chosen Arduino pins — use SoftwareSerial if you need the hardware serial for uploads. In your sketch implement a simple parser that reads incoming bytes and acts on '1' and '0'. Test pairing from a Bluetooth terminal app and send the characters. If the LED doesn’t toggle, check wiring, ensure you used the correct RX/TX orientation, and verify the baud rate matches the module. A common troubleshooting step is to open the Serial Monitor and echo incoming bytes to confirm the module is sending what you expect. Why this exercise matters: it ties wiring, serial parsing, and user interaction together in a small, verifiable loop and gives a clear verification milestone. Misconception check: this is not the same as a secured remote control — it’s a local, paired control mechanism for learning. After success, consider how you would harden the interface for wider deployment.

screens.title: Assessing board choice and tradeoffs
screens.narratorSegment: A good assessment question tests whether you can compare platforms and justify a choice. For example, ask: what is the main advantage of using an ESP32 instead of an Arduino Uno with an ESP8266 add‑on module? Then contrast how an Uno plus an external module requires bridging and can introduce serial and wiring complexity. Takeaway: evaluate projects by required network features, memory, and development convenience when choosing between architectures. fullNarratorScript:
Wireless communication is the step that turns an Arduino project into an Internet of Things device. In this chapter you'll learn how simple serial Bluetooth modules like the HC-05 and HC-06 behave like ordinary serial ports, how to wire and talk to them safely, and how to use an ESP8266 or ESP32 board when you need built‑in Wi‑Fi. We'll walk through the hands‑on flow: wiring a Bluetooth module, pairing it with a phone, sending on/off commands, and then contrast that with running a tiny web server on an ESP board to control an LED from a browser. You'll also learn the security basics you must consider before exposing controls over the air, including why hard‑coding passwords is fine for experiments but risky for real devices. To ground learning, there are concrete examples: a Bluetooth controlled LED using simple serial commands, and the minimal ESP8266 web server sketch that serves a control page. As you go through each lesson, notice a common tradeoff: Bluetooth modules are simple and low cost; ESP boards offer more memory and network features. Think about which option matches your project goals and what security steps you would add before deploying.

By the end of this chapter you will be able to add simple wireless control to a microcontroller project, and you will know when to choose Bluetooth or a Wi‑Fi board. First, you will connect an HC‑05 or HC‑06 to an Arduino and treat it as a serial device, using the same send and receive functions you already know. That skill matters because it lets you control pins and devices from a phone without changing how your sketch parses input. Second, you will set up SoftwareSerial when the hardware serial pins are reserved for USB programming, a practical workaround that prevents conflicts during development. Third, you will identify when an ESP8266 or ESP32 board is the better platform — these boards have built‑in Wi‑Fi and more memory, so they run web servers and handle networked logic more easily. Finally, you will apply basic IoT security checks: avoid exposing unauthenticated controls, avoid publishing hard‑coded credentials in production, and plan for firmware updates. Each objective includes a short hands‑on checkpoint so you can confirm competency as you build.

Let's map the objectives to real project actions so you understand why each skill matters. When you link an HC‑05 to an Arduino, you are exposing the same serial input path used by the USB monitor, but now the input can come from a phone. That means your parsing code stays the same and your UI options expand to mobile apps and inexpensive Bluetooth terminals. SoftwareSerial matters because pins zero and one are commonly used for USB programming; if you accidentally wire a Bluetooth TX to the hardware RX while uploading sketches you may block uploads or get confusing serial data. Choosing an ESP8266 or ESP32 replaces the Uno plus wireless add‑on pattern with a single board that has built‑in Wi‑Fi and more memory. That simplifies web server projects and frees you from bridging serial links. Finally, the security objective ties everything together: whether you control an LED over Bluetooth or a web page, exposing unauthenticated control to the public internet is risky. Practically, we will test each objective with a hands‑on exercise and a small verification step so you can confirm competency.

A Bluetooth module such as the HC‑05 or HC‑06 acts like a wireless serial cable. In practice this means you can use the same send and receive routines you already use with USB: the print function to send text and the read functions to receive it. Concretely, if your sketch looks for the string on to switch an LED on, you can keep that logic unchanged and have a phone send the string instead of the Serial Monitor. This is powerful because it separates the transport from your application logic. A common misconception is that Bluetooth modules require special wireless APIs; they do not — they simply forward bytes over a radio link. One caution: the HC‑05 has pins labeled VCC, GND, TXD, RXD, EN, and STATE, and TX/RX lines operate at microcontroller logic levels. If you wire TXD directly into a 5V Arduino RX without a level check you may risk damage; use a simple voltage divider when required. Example: sending the characters "on" from a phone terminal app can trigger the same conditional code you use for a typed command. Takeaway: treat Bluetooth modules as serial wires that happen to be wireless, and mind pin voltages and hardware serial conflicts as you wire and program.

Wiring a Bluetooth module correctly keeps your hardware safe and your project reliable. The HC‑05 typically exposes six pins: VCC, GND, TXD, RXD, EN, and STATE. VCC powers the module; GND is the common reference. TXD transmits bytes from the module and connects to the Arduino receive pin; RXD receives bytes from the Arduino and connects to the Arduino transmit pin. A practical safety step is checking voltage levels: many Arduino boards use five volt logic while some Bluetooth modules expect three point three volts. That means you should use a simple voltage divider on the Arduino TX line going to RXD when required, or ensure the module tolerates five volts. The EN pin can be used to enable or disable the module, useful in power management, and STATE provides a status output that some projects use to detect pairing. A common wiring mistake is swapping TX and RX incorrectly or powering the module with the wrong voltage. Example wiring: VCC to 5V, GND to ground, TXD to Arduino RX via direct or divider as required, RXD to Arduino TX — but if you plan to upload sketches, avoid pins zero and one and use SoftwareSerial on other digital pins. Takeaway: double‑check pin labels, voltage, and choose SoftwareSerial when USB programming must remain available.

Hardware serial pins on many Arduino models are shared with the USB interface, so a popular pattern is to use SoftwareSerial or similar libraries to move Bluetooth communication to other digital pins. The core idea is simple: create a secondary serial object attached to two free digital pins, and read and write to it just like the hardware serial. This lets the USB port remain free for programming and for the Serial Monitor so you can debug while the Bluetooth module runs in parallel. A common mistake is assuming SoftwareSerial works at very high baud rates; performance can degrade, so test your chosen baud and reduce it if you see dropped characters. Example process: choose two free pins, initialize SoftwareSerial at the module's baud rate, swap TX/RX as needed, then implement the same parsing logic you use for Serial. Why it matters: using SoftwareSerial prevents upload conflicts and keeps your development loop fast. Misconception check: SoftwareSerial is not faster or more reliable than hardware serial; it's a practical workaround for development convenience. Takeaway: use SoftwareSerial for development when hardware serial is busy, and verify stability at your chosen baud rate before finalizing wiring.

Pairing an HC‑05 or HC‑06 with a smartphone creates a virtual serial link that your phone can send strings over. The typical flow is: power the module, make it discoverable or enter pairing mode, pair from the phone using a Bluetooth terminal app, then open a terminal to send commands. In many learning projects you will send short commands like "on" and "off" or single characters like "1" and "0" to represent states. Your sketch looks for those exact strings and sets digital outputs accordingly. A practical example: if you send the character "1" the sketch sets an LED pin HIGH; if you send "0" the sketch sets it LOW. A common misconception is that pairing alone secures control; it does not prevent someone already paired from sending dangerous commands. For this reason, keep critical controls on authenticated channels or limit pairing range when possible. When testing, start with simple commands, confirm the LED or relay responds, and then expand to richer command parsing only after you validate reliability. Takeaway: pairing creates convenience but not full security — start simple, then plan safeguards.

The Arduino Uno itself lacks built‑in Wi‑Fi. You have two common paths to add network capability: connect an ESP8266 module to an Uno, or use an ESP8266‑based board such as NodeMCU or a Wemos D1 Mini, or choose an ESP32 board. The key tradeoffs are convenience, resources, and complexity. An Uno with an ESP8266 add‑on keeps your familiar Uno environment but adds wiring, serial bridging, and potential baud or pin conflicts. By contrast, using a NodeMCU or ESP32 replaces the Uno with a single board that already has Wi‑Fi, more memory, and higher speed. That makes serving web pages and handling network logic simpler and more robust. A common misconception is that the Uno plus module and the NodeMCU are identical experiences; they are not — the latter simplifies networking and avoids bridging problems. Example: an ESP board can run the same Arduino language sketches and libraries while offering a built‑in network stack to host a web server. Practical guidance: prefer ESP boards for web server projects and when you need memory and speed; use an Uno plus ESP module if you have peripherals tied to the Uno and need minimal wireless features. Takeaway: choose the architecture that matches your resource, wiring, and deployment needs.

The provided sketch shows the essential steps: include the Wi‑Fi and server libraries, provide network credentials, wait for a connection, register a handler for the root path, and start the server loop. The sketch sets the LED pin as output, connects to the network using the provided network name and password, waits until the board reports it is connected, and then registers a handler function for the root URL that sends a web page with on/off controls. The loop then calls the server handle function to respond to client requests. Important practical points: hard‑coding credentials is acceptable for learning and quick testing but not recommended for devices that will be deployed. Also, the ESP family boards run the same Arduino language, so you can reuse familiar functions but now you also get the networking APIs. A common misconception is that web servers require complex frameworks; the ESP8266 can serve simple pages with a few library calls. Takeaway: this minimal sketch demonstrates the flow of connecting, registering handlers, and serving pages — enough to build interactive control pages for LEDs and simple peripherals.
